title: Is cognitive functioning impaired in methamphetamine users? A critical review

claims.statement: In adults with a history of heavy methamphetamine use, scanned after days to months of abstinence, striatal dopamine transporter availability is lower on average than in people who do not use: about 20–28% lower in individual PET studies, and a pooled standardized difference of g = −1.47 (95% CI −1.83 to −1.10; 9 studies, 108 users, 126 controls). Individual values overlap with the control range, and these designs cannot show whether the difference reflects lost nerve terminals, reduced transporter expression or differences that predate use.
claims.magnitude: Individual PET studies: caudate −27.8% and putamen −21.1% (15 users vs 18 controls); caudate −23% and putamen −25% (6 vs 10). Pooled: g −1.47 (95% CI −1.83 to −1.10), 9 studies of amphetamine-type stimulant users. Group distributions overlap.

claims.statement: In five adults from a treatment programme who were scanned after about 3 months of abstinence and again after about 14 months, striatal dopamine transporter availability rose by 19% in the caudate and 16% in the putamen; in the same programme, people abstinent for a similar time (n=10) did not differ significantly from controls, whereas those in short abstinence (n=12) were 21–26% lower. The five who stayed abstinent started with higher transporter levels than those who dropped out, no control group was rescanned, and another PET study found no relation between abstinence duration and transporter levels.
claims.magnitude: Within-person: +19% caudate, +16% putamen (n=5). Cross-sectional: protracted abstinence 5% (caudate) and 9% (putamen) below controls, not significant (n=10 vs 11; editors' standardized difference about −0.3 and −0.6, so a moderate remaining difference is not excluded); short abstinence 26% and 21% below.

claims.statement: In one PET study, 15 people abstinent from methamphetamine had 14% higher whole-brain glucose metabolism than 21 controls (p<0.05, while the study set p<0.01 as its threshold), with relatively lower metabolism in the thalamus (17%) and striatum (6–12%); another research group found no difference in global metabolism. Users and controls also differed in smoking (73% vs 24%) and sex ratio, and cognition was tested in users only.
claims.magnitude: Whole brain 38.4 vs 33.6 µmol/100 g/min (+14%, t=2.2, df=34, p<0.05); relative to whole brain: thalamus −17%, caudate −12%, putamen −6%, parietal +5%. Not replicated for global metabolism by London et al. (2004).

claims.statement: Whether methamphetamine use, as people use it, causes lasting loss of or damage to dopamine neurons in humans has not been established: lower dopamine markers in heavy users are consistently found, but the measures available cannot distinguish loss of nerve terminals from reversible down-regulation, some markers return toward normal with abstinence, and the pattern differs from that of Parkinson's disease.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable: no study has counted dopamine neurons or terminals quantitatively in human users.

claims.statement: In the same laboratory studies, single intranasal doses improved some measures of attention and psychomotor speed (divided-attention tracking at all doses; digit-symbol substitution at the two smaller of three doses) and did not significantly worsen any measured task; a review of 16 controlled single-dose studies reached the same conclusion. The studies were too small to exclude small impairments, and repeated or binge use was not tested.
claims.magnitude: Improvement on divided-attention measures at all active doses and on digit-symbol substitution at 12 and 25 but not 50 mg/70 kg; no significant change on repeated acquisition, rapid information processing or digit recall; no residual effects at 24 h. Effect sizes not reported (values in figures only).

claims.statement: Average test scores of groups of people who use methamphetamine mostly fall in the low-average to average range of population norms, and a minority of users meet conventional impairment criteria, more often than controls: about 7 of 27 users versus 2 of 18 controls met a 2-SD criterion in at least one domain in one study, and 34% of users versus 16% of controls were classified as globally impaired in another.
claims.magnitude: Group means between about the 16th and 55th percentiles on normed tests (Simon et al., 2010); impaired in at least one domain 7/27 (26%) vs 2/18 (11%) (Kalechstein et al., 2003, as reported by Hart et al., 2012); globally impaired 34% vs 16% (Iudicello et al., 2010).

claims.statement: Whether methamphetamine use causes lasting cognitive impairment in humans has not been established: users score lower than non-users on average, but no study has measured cognition before use began, groups differ in education and other risk factors, and the differences have not been shown to change with abstinence more than practice effects do.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable from current designs; the size of the association is given in the claim on group differences (section 9).
